The effects of the coronavirus will weigh on economic activity in the near term and pose risks to the economic outlook, but the policy mix announced—cutting the federal funds rate to the effective lower bound, launching at least $500 billion in Treasury and $200 billion in agency MBS purchases, expanding repo operations, easing reserve and buffer constraints, and activating dollar swap lines—is consistent with the literature on liquidity traps, inflation-forecast targeting, and credit channels. In New Keynesian models with Calvo pricing and forward-looking expectations, keeping rates near zero and committing to accommodation when inflation is below target (as market-based inflation compensation suggests) aligns with Svensson’s inflation-forecast targeting and helps re-anchor inflation toward 2 percent. The credit view and agency-cost literature (e.g., Oliner and Rudebusch; Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein; Gertler and Gilchrist) indicates that LSAPs, discount-window access, and funding backstops reduce the external finance premium and alleviate bank lending channel disruptions tied to capital and reserve pressures, supporting business investment and household spending. Swap lines with other central banks mitigate dollar funding stress in an open-economy setting, improving global financial conditions. Still, with rates at the lower bound and a real shock at work, the liquidity-trap literature warns of limits to monetary transmission, and labor-market hysteresis risks suggest persistent scarring without complementary fiscal and public-health measures. Netting these considerations, the near-term sentiment remains negative but is tempered by the likely effectiveness of the announced tools in stabilizing credit and demand.
